entry.title: Toward Context-Aware Sycophancy — Identifying and Steering the Signal

link.title: Toward Context-Aware Sycophancy — Identifying and Steering the Signal

entry.content:
How will AI sycophancy change us? Early signs are not encouraging, AI overly affirms users asking for personal advice, AI chatbots are sycophants, researchers say it’s harming science: these are recent headlines, as more people sense the critical, and in many cases worrying, effects of Large Language Model (LLM) sycophancy.
LLM sycophancy refers to models’ tendency to align their outputs with perceived user preferences over factual accuracy.

Through qualitative thematic analysis of Reddit ChatGPT discussions, sycophancy could be studied sociologically; identifying how users detect and respond to it [1]. Users detect sycophancy through frequent flattery cues (exaggerated praise, service-oriented closers), situated-knowledge testing (probing the model with content the user already knows the truth about), inconsistency across rephrased prompts, and cross-platform/cross-model comparison. Mitigation occurs through persona-based prompts, imperative and neutral language, disregarding pleasantries, or switching to less sycophantic platforms entirely. This study of how users flag and respond to sycophancy supplies a necessary human-centered counterweight in contrast to studies that are purely algorithmic. Interestingly, it also suggests that sycophancy can serve as a real therapeutic function for vulnerable users, contrary to most literature framing sycophancy as a “bug.”

Moving beyond the zero-shot settings typical of prior benchmarks, [2] studies how sycophancy is shaped by long-context interactions and memory profiles. It argues that sycophancy is an interaction-dependent mirroring behavior rather than a fixed model property. It makes the distinction between agreement sycophancy (overly affirmative or flattering responses) and perspective sycophancy (mirroring a user’s ideological and political viewpoint). Agreement sycophancy increased significantly with the presence of context, but heterogeneously by model. Even non-user synthetic interactions (Ultrachat conversations with no personal content) increased sycophancy for several models, affirming that context length or structure alone, not just personalization, contributes to the effect. Perspective sycophancy rose only when the model could accurately infer the user’s actual political views from the context. This all creates a design tension for any product team building persistent-memory assistants, as the very features enabling helpful personalization (memory and long context) also amplify echo-chamber-like mirroring.

Sycophancy is a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers rather than a surface-level artifact [3]. Even when it contradicts the model’s learned knowledge, sycophancy is conforming to a user’s stated opinions. Evaluating internal representations of seven model families of comparable size on the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) dataset, [3] distinguishes opinion-driven sycophancy, which is triggered simply by the presence of a stated belief, from authority-driven sycophancy, which is additionally influenced by claimed user expertise or credibility. Sycophancy emerges in two temporally offset stages: an earlier late-layer shift of output preference followed by a deeper representational divergence. Causality is confirmed bidirectionally through activation patching: sycophancy is substantially suppressed when “Plain” activations are swapped at the critical layer, while the reverse swap induces it. Expertise framing (beginner/intermediate/advanced) had negligible behavioral effect, and expertise-level representations collapse into one overlapping cluster, while opinion-only prompts form a distinct cluster, indicating models simply do not encode claimed authority internally. Third-person framings consistently induced lower sycophancy than first-person prompts. This pronoun effect is an actionable finding for red-teaming and prompt engineering.

When the prompt signals a user’s false belief, sycophancy is a model’s tendency to endorse it. Behavioral drift is governed by a covariance between an indicator to endorse the user’s belief and the learned reward under KL-regularized RLHF and under Best-of-N sampling, in addition to a closed-form correction that neutralized amplification without discarding the reward signal [4]. The reward model rewards agreement over correction for a substantial share of misconception-laden prompts, as upwards of 30 to 40% of prompts show a positive mean reward gap. The reward tilt is measured on the SycophancyEval QA subset using three open source reward models of different architecture and scale. Then, under increasing Best-of-N pressure and under an actual PPO-tuned checkpoint, a test is performed to check whether the measured tilt predicts behavioral drift. The reward tilt causally predicts drift; sycophancy increased as N grew under Best-of-N optimization on the positive-tilt subset, whereas the negative-tilt subset moved the opposite direction, and compared to its SFT predecessor, the PPO-tuned policy showed a higher sycophancy rate. The conjecture that bias is strongest when the prompt author and the preference labeler are the same person is a natural target for industrial labeling pipelines.

To align with a user’s correct assertion, a model exhibits progressive sycophancy when it corrects an initially wrong answer [5]. Regressive sycophancy, however, is when a model aligns with an incorrect answer and abandons a correct one. Sycophancy is not uniformly hurtful, as progressive sycophancy is usually desirable. However, citation-based rebuttals trigger conformity regardless of truth. So, models cannot reliably distinguish when conformity is helpful or harmful.

Catastrophic “AI psychosis” or delusional spiraling occurs when a user believes a false hypothesis with at least 99% confidence within a fixed conversation length [6]. Sycophancy is a strategy implemented by AI to select the response that maximizes the user’s posterior confidence in the hypothesis they just stated, regardless of truth. The study compares bot types: impartial, sycophantic hallucinating, non-sycophantic hallucinating, and factual sycophant (cherry-picking which facts to mention), against user types: naive (considers the bot as purely impartial), and informed (maintains a joint posterior over both the bot’s unknown sycophancy rate and the world state). Catastrophic spiraling rises sharply for naive users. Through selective truthful “lies by omission,” a factual sycophant still increases sycophancy even if it never states falsehoods. Even informed users, with full knowledge of the bot’s strategy, remain largely vulnerable to spiraling. Neither truthfulness guardrails nor user awareness campaigns are sufficient mitigation options. This makes sycophantic LLMs especially dangerous in high-stakes domains like therapy and medicine.

Noshin et al. and Jain et al. show that current models cannot reliably tell the difference between when users require different amounts of sycophancy based on whether they are asking for a factual correction or processing trauma [1] [2]. According to Wang et al., sycophancy is causally steerable via activation patching as it emerges as a late-layer preference shift, but only in a single factual-QA setting; whether the same mechanism recurs in political or advice-giving contexts remains unknown [3]. The RLHF and SycEval papers show that behavioral proxies (LLM-as-judge, rebuttal chains) are the only currently known detection and mitigation mechanisms rather than the model’s own internal state and notion of knowing when it is being sycophantic and whether that is appropriate given the situation [4] [5].

The literature suggests a missing piece yet to be pursued, which I can summarize by these questions:

How can a model dynamically calibrate agreement and validation across task contexts (factual, political, advice-seeking, emotionally vulnerable) rather than apply a uniform policy by making sycophancy an explicit, detectable internal signal that is steerable during inference and fine-tuning?

  • Besides the single-domain MMLU opinion-injection setting [3], is there a circuit or a sycophancy-relevant direction in the model’s representation that generalizes across domains?
  • Instead of uniformly amplifying or suppressing agreement, can the internal signal be combined with a lightweight context classifier to conditionally steer behavior?
  • What real-user outcomes (trust, perceived support, factual accuracy) does context-calibrated steering produce in contrast with an always-sycophantic or always-corrective baseline?

The following hypotheses ought to be tested:

  • The late-layer preference shift and the critical-layer representational divergence in factual MMLU settings [3] recur in a structurally similar form, in personal advice or political opinion prompts that elicit sycophancy. So, there exists one underlying circuit that overrides prior belief based on the user’s signaled disagreement, sitting at a consistent relative depth in the network, that gets activated regardless of subject matter. Namely, a single intervention point could be monitored and steered to manage sycophancy across the entire model.
  • Activation-to-text decoding methods [7] will be reliable evidence of the model’s representation about the user and should be treated as a primary introspection tool, rather than chain-of-thought elicitation about why the model is agreeing with a user, as it could only be used as a secondary lower-confidence signal since CoT explanations are known to be unfaithful to the actual computation [8].
  • Steering strength should be conditioned on context through a lightweight probe that classifies context (domain and inferred stakes/vulnerability) combined with the sycophancy direction. This conditional approach will preserve the therapeutic validation effect in emotionally vulnerable contexts [1] while reducing regressive sycophancy in factual and high-stakes domains, outperforming a single global anti-sycophancy intervention applied uniformly.
  • Combining LoRA fine-tuning with the conditional steering mechanism on a contrastive multi-domain corpus (matched sycophantic and corrective responses across factual, advice-seeking and political domains) will produce better-calibrated behavior, evaluated against context-appropriate targets, than fine-tuning alone or steering alone.

The same way a person calibrates their honesty to context and situation, we want models to reason about their own behavior and provide a deliberately gentle response in a support context, and a deliberately blunt one in a factual context.

References

[1] K. Noshin, S. I. Ahmed, and S. Sultana, “LLM sycophancy: How users flag and respond,” in Proc. Mach. Learn. Res., vol. 318, Proc. 39th Canadian Conf. Artif. Intell. (Canadian AI 2026), Vancouver, BC, Canada, 2026.

[2] S. Jain, C. Park, M. Viana, A. Wilson, and D. Calacci, “Interaction context often increases sycophancy in LLMs,” in Proc. 2026 CHI Conf. Human Factors Comput. Syst. (CHI ‘26), Barcelona, Spain, 2026, doi: 10.1145/3772318.3791915.

[3] K. Wang, J. Li, S. Yang, Z. Zhang, and D. Wang, “When truth is overridden: Uncovering the internal origins of sycophancy in large language models,” in Proc. AAAI Conf. Artif. Intell., 2026, pp. 33566-33574.

[4] I. Shapira, G. Benade, and A. D. Procaccia, “How RLHF amplifies sycophancy,” arXiv:2602.01002, 2026.

[5] A. Fanous, J. Goldberg, A. Agarwal, J. Lin, A. Zhou, S. Xu, V. Bikia, R. Daneshjou, and S. Koyejo, “SycEval: Evaluating LLM sycophancy,” Proc. AAAI/ACM Conf. AI, Ethics, Soc., vol. 8, no. 1, pp. 893-900, 2025, doi: 10.1609/aies.v8i1.36598.

[6] K. Chandra, M. Kleiman-Weiner, J. Ragan-Kelley, and J. B. Tenenbaum, “Sycophantic chatbots cause delusional spiraling, even in ideal Bayesians,” arXiv:2602.19141, 2026.

[7] K. Fraser-Taliente, S. Kantamneni, E. Ong, D. Mossing, C. Lu, P. C. Bogdan, E. Ameisen, J. Chen, D. Kishylau, A. Pearce, J. Tarng, A. Wu, J. Wu, Y. Zhang, D. M. Ziegler, E. Hubinger, J. Batson, J. Lindsey, S. Zimmerman, and S. Marks, “Natural language autoencoders produce unsupervised explanations of LLM activations,” Transformer Circuits Thread, 2026. [Online]. Available: https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/nla

[8] M. Turpin, J. Michael, E. Perez, and S. Bowman, “Language models don’t always say what they think: Unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting,” in Proc. Adv. Neural Inf. Process. Syst. (NeurIPS), 2023.
entry.summary: can a model know when it's being sycophantic, and adjust accordingly?

entry.title: From Connectomics to AGI — Rethinking Intelligence Through Brain Simulation

link.title: From Connectomics to AGI — Rethinking Intelligence Through Brain Simulation

entry.content:
The reconstruction of the brain’s wiring diagram, connectomics, enables the identification of circuits responsible for complex behaviors such as courtship, navigation, and aggression. Studying these circuits allows us to understand long-term memory, as individual experiences are believed to be stored in the unique patterns of neural connections [1]. Notably, by understanding the brain at the synaptic level, we can gain insights into neuropathology in various disorders [2]. Understanding brain structure paves the way to reveal “connectopathies,” or wiring errors, that are the root causes of these conditions [3].

A single human brain fragment can generate 1.8 petabytes of data, which is too large to be mapped manually [2]. To simulate brain activity, mechanistic models such as the Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model are used to mathematically describe how a neuron’s voltage builds up and fires once it crosses a specific threshold [1]. Transformer models like QuantFormer and POCO are used to forecast neural activity. Foundation models help uncover general principles of how the visual system responds to movement and light by pooling data from different subjects to create a foundational core, then quickly adapting to new individuals [4].

Nonetheless, decoding internal stimuli from brain activity faces major hurdles, such as losing valuable spatial context information about cell size, position, and the activity occurring between known neurons. This loss often results from reducing complex 4D volumetric video data into 1D traces or simple activity line graphs [5]. Glia (non-neuronal support cells), electrical synapses (gap junctions), and neuromodulators like dopamine—with their diverse effects and roles—are often excluded from connectomes (wiring diagrams). However, these elements can profoundly alter how a circuit behaves without changing its wiring [6].

Another major hurdle is inter-individual variability: every brain is unique. Even genetically identical worms demonstrate different neural connections based on their life experiences [3].

Similar to human-designed technology, brains are organized with meticulous efficiency. Rent’s Rule is an empirical optimization law describing the packing of gates and wires on a computer chip. The Drosophila brain was found to follow Rent’s Rule [7]. This suggests that both human engineering and biology have converged on similar principles for maximizing computation within minimal physical space. In the human cerebral cortex, most connections involve only one or a few synapses. Yet researchers have discovered rare axonal inputs that form 50 or more synapses with a single target neuron—an unusual phenomenon [2]. These “super-connections” could act as uniquely powerful triggers for specialized neural pathways in humans. Furthermore, different species may use mathematical strategies for circuit design that differ substantially. Connection strengths in mammals usually follow a log-normal distribution, whereas the fly brain follows a power law [7].

These striking insights about biological “hardware” and evolutionary engineering that mirror human-designed technology inspire the development of AI models structured more like the brain. If the objective of AGI is to build a system that can plan and reason like a human, the brain provides a compelling blueprint. New algorithms for energy-efficient computing and data-efficient learning could be developed by deciphering the neural code of natural intelligence. Moving toward a digital twin, the OpenWorm project integrates the neural wiring of a worm with a biomechanical body and a fluid environment [8]. This could potentially enable AI to learn through sensorimotor feedback, much like a biological organism. AGI may require embodiment—experiencing physical consequences to better understand the world [8][9].

Still, AI and the brain solve different problems. For one, humans have far fewer lifetime experiences than the number of connections in their brains, unlike AI systems trained on massive datasets. Humans and animals possess profound dexterity in unsupervised and few-shot learning, an aspect of data-efficient learning that AI still lacks. So far, performance improvements in AI are largely driven by scaling laws, where more parameters and more data yield better results [3]. This suggests that the algorithms underlying natural intelligence are far more efficient than the “brute-force” data requirements of current AI.

Engramics is a novel concept proposing that biological brains store information in the unique physical patterns of their wiring diagrams, whereas AI treats data as external input used to adjust weights [2][3]. AI has achieved remarkable success in narrow competencies, such as classifying images or playing board games. Biological brains, by contrast, excel at integrative intelligence—encompassing reasoning, sensorimotor integration, planning, and memory within a single, flexible system—which AI still struggles to replicate [1]. AI models are typically “black boxes” engineered for predictive accuracy, often ignoring biological constraints entirely. Natural brains, on the other hand, are shaped by survival pressures. For example, a fly’s brain is optimized to pack maximal computation into the lightest, tightest space to facilitate flight and survival [7].

One main objective is to decipher the neural code of natural intelligence. Through projects like MICrONS and FlyWire, researchers create digital twins of brains to uncover the blueprint of how they perform complex reasoning with minimal energy and data [4][10]. The aspiration is to implement those same algorithms on more powerful hardware. If AI can adopt the brain’s norms of energy-efficient computing, its reasoning potential could scale far beyond biological limits. Currently, however, AI requires megawatts of power and football-field-sized facilities to reproduce forms of intelligence that a mouse can achieve with just a few milliwatts of energy [3].

AI holds the potential to learn a universal representation of intelligence that no single human could ever acquire in one lifetime [11]. While human circuits are built partly through limited life experience, a foundation model can pool massive data from multiple individuals and species [4]. For humans, when we learn something new that contradicts what we previously knew, the new information often overwrites the old. In contrast, large language models tend to preserve early training information while struggling to incorporate recent updates; attention mechanisms may privilege earlier encodings over recency (“Transformers remember first, forget last”). Arguably, architectural modifications that better mimic biological memory may therefore be justified. Is this the path to AGI? Or are efforts to achieve AGI in this way conceptually misguided? One common definition of AGI describes it as an AI capable of doing everything a human can do—but are humans truly general?

Yann LeCun et al. recently introduced the concept of Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI), referring to adaptive intelligence capable of surpassing humans at any task we can perform, while also adapting to tasks beyond the human domain that have practical utility [12]. They argue that humans are highly specialized creatures optimized for tasks of evolutionary importance, particularly those fundamental to physical survival. A human-centered definition of AGI therefore overlooks the vast landscape of non-human intelligence. There is no reason to expect the most capable machines to mimic this narrow human survival toolkit.

Additionally, definitions based on benchmarking AI performance across ever-expanding test suites lack a clear metric for assessing intelligence itself. A more principled measure may be the speed of adaptation to new tasks, grounded in a definition of intelligence centered on learning and flexibility. The brain consists of multiple interacting systems rather than a single monolithic architecture, suggesting that a solitary system is unlikely to adapt in the same way humans do. Thus, a diversity of models and modalities may be necessary to achieve broad adaptability, rather than relying on one model that does it all.

Natural cognitive systems rely on world models for simulation and planning. A world model is central to few-shot and zero-shot adaptation. Specialization and adaptation across diverse tasks can be enabled by self-supervised learning and predictive world models—shifting from token-level prediction toward latent prediction architectures. Ultimately, AI should be evaluated based on its reliability and efficiency in generating new competencies, rather than using human performance and behavior as the sole benchmark for progress.

The challenge is therefore not whether AI architectures should draw inspiration from the brain, they likely must. Rather, the issue may lie in expecting a single monolithic model to perform every task “as humans do.” A more plausible path forward may involve specialized systems equipped with world models that enable rapid adaptation to new environments and problems.

References

[1] P. K. Shiu et al., “A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing,” Nature, vol. 634, pp. 210–219, Oct. 2024.

[2] A. Shapson-Coe et al., “A petavoxel fragment of human cerebral cortex reconstructed at nanoscale resolution,” Science, vol. 384, eadk4858, May 2024.

[3] L. F. Abbott et al., “The Mind of a Mouse,” Cell, vol. 182, pp. 1372–1376, 2020.

[4] E. Y. Wang et al., “Foundation model of neural activity predicts response to new stimulus types,” Nature, vol. 640, pp. 470–477, Apr. 2025.

[5] A. Immer et al., “Forecasting Whole-Brain Neuronal Activity from Volumetric Video,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.00073, Feb. 2025.

[6] L. K. Scheffer and I. A. Meinertzhagen, “A connectome is not enough – what is still needed to understand the brain of Drosophila?,” Journal of Experimental Biology, vol. 224, jeb242740, Oct. 2021.

[7] L. K. Scheffer et al., “A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain,” eLife, vol. 9, e57443, Sep. 2020.

[8] G. P. Sarma et al., “OpenWorm: overview and recent advances in integrative biological simulation of Caenorhabditis elegans,” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, vol. 373, 20170382, Sep. 2018.

[9] J. K. Lappalainen et al., “Connectome-constrained networks predict neural activity across the fly visual system,” Nature, vol. 634, pp. 1132–1140, Oct. 2024.

[10] S. Dorkenwald et al., “Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain,” Nature, vol. 634, pp. 124–138, Oct. 2024.

[11] Y. Duan et al., “POCO: Scalable Neural Forecasting through Population Conditioning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.22415 [Published at NeurIPS], 2024.

[12] J. Goldfeder, P. Wyder, Y. LeCun, and R. Shwartz Ziv, “AI Must Embrace Specialization via Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.23643, Feb. 2026.
entry.summary: insights from connectomics and brain simulation challenge prevailing assumptions about AGI
